# Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics — concept pack (small)

> Source-anchored research for Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics. Run status: COMPLETED.

<!-- generated by llms-concept-abstractor v1.4.1 · generated 2026-11-09 · budgeted to ≈8000 tokens; the full catalogue is llms-full.txt -->

## Structure and components

- [statement] Plan accessible venues or remote participation, transportation, breaks and usable materials as part of recruitment logistics; budget participant payments and access-related expenses. (medium confidence) — https://www.section508.gov/develop/usability-testing-with-people-with-disabilities/ · keywords: Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/

## How it works

- [statement] Disability advocacy groups, community organizations and specialist accessibility panels provide recruitment channels. When using an agency, check its disability recruitment experience and specify the actual access needs relevant to the study. (medium confidence) — https://www.section508.gov/develop/usability-testing-with-people-with-disabilities/ · keywords: Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://tetralogical.com/blog/2022/08/01/inclusive-user-research-recruiting-participants/
- [statement] Treat consent as continuing: remind participants that participation is voluntary and check again when they appear uncomfortable or confused; allow withdrawal without forfeiting the promised incentive. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/getting-users-consent-for-research · keywords: Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/
- [statement] Explain any practical cutoff for withdrawing already anonymised or published data. Cambridge’s Inclusive Design Toolkit specifically advises disclosing when later withdrawal becomes impossible. (low confidence) — https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/
- [statement] Offer consent materials in usable formats and provide a documented verbal-consent route when appropriate; a handwritten signature is not the only way these guides describe recording consent. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/getting-users-consent-for-research · keywords: Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/
- [statement] Explain that participation is voluntary and withdrawal is permitted; GOV.UK additionally advises checking continued consent when a participant seems uncomfortable or confused. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/getting-users-consent-for-research · keywords: Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/
- [statement] The guides scope post-session withdrawal differently: GOV.UK prescribes deletion on withdrawal, while Cambridge explicitly addresses limits after anonymisation or repository publication. Treat these as attributed guidance and explain the study-specific withdrawal process and limits in advance. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/getting-users-consent-for-research · keywords: Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/

## How-to and procedures

- [statement] Use data within the consent obtained, minimize personal data collection, protect stored data and explain sharing and recordings to participants. (medium confidence) — https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/ · keywords: Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/getting-users-consent-for-research

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] For disability-inclusive recruitment, specify functional access needs, assistive technology and devices rather than relying on diagnosis labels; match recruitment criteria to likely barriers in the product. (medium confidence) — https://www.section508.gov/develop/usability-testing-with-people-with-disabilities/ · keywords: Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://tetralogical.com/blog/2022/08/01/inclusive-user-research-recruiting-participants/
- [statement] Nielsen Norman Group cautions that convenience samples, coworkers and existing-customer panels can bias feedback or omit new-user perspectives; select channels against the study question rather than convenience alone. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/recruiting-screening-research-candidates/
- [statement] For children, adults with consent-related support needs, or methods where ordinary consent is impractical, consult specific ethical guidance and the rules of the relevant countries rather than extending a generic UX consent template uncritically. (low confidence) — https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/
- [statement] Section508.gov advises screening for functional needs, assistive technology, typical devices and technology comfort rather than medical diagnoses. (low confidence) — https://www.section508.gov/develop/usability-testing-with-people-with-disabilities/
- [statement] Budget participant compensation and participation costs rather than treating access expenses as incidental: Cambridge recommends reimbursing out-of-pocket costs, while Section508.gov includes incentives, travel support and separate attendant reimbursement. (medium confidence) — https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/ · keywords: Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://www.section508.gov/develop/usability-testing-with-people-with-disabilities/
- [statement] Great Question cautions that much academic incentive-bias research concerns surveys and clinical trials rather than moderated UX interviews; this limits direct generalization to UX sessions. (low confidence) — https://www.greatquestion.com/blog/how-do-incentives-impact-bias-in-ux-research

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Recruit across the target population’s backgrounds and abilities, and track which segments have been missed; choose recruitment criteria using the product’s users, research objectives and likely barriers. (medium confidence) — https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/ · keywords: Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://tetralogical.com/blog/2022/08/01/inclusive-user-research-recruiting-participants/, https://www.nngroup.com/articles/recruiting-screening-research-candidates/
- [statement] Screeners should establish relevant experience without unnecessary exclusion rules. Nielsen Norman Group recommends avoiding questions that reveal the desired answer and reviewing responses from both qualified and disqualified candidates. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/recruiting-screening-research-candidates/
- [statement] Obtain consent through understandable information and a voluntary decision: explain the study purpose, activities, data use and sharing, recording, and the right to stop; allow time for questions. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/getting-users-consent-for-research · keywords: Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/
- [statement] Make consent accessible in both language and format. GOV.UK offers reading aloud, assistive-technology-compatible digital forms and recorded verbal consent as practical alternatives; Indeed recommends checking understanding in participants’ own words. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/getting-users-consent-for-research · keywords: Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://indeed.design/article/three-basic-principles-of-ethical-research-that-ux-can-take-from-academia/
- [statement] Keep evidence of what each participant consented to and match that record to the corresponding research data. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/getting-users-consent-for-research
- [statement] Minimise personal data collection and protect confidentiality; removing names alone may leave participants identifiable through characteristics or quotations, especially in small recruitment pools. (medium confidence) — https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/ · keywords: Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://www.section508.gov/develop/usability-testing-with-people-with-disabilities/
- [statement] Prepare a response for participant distress or unsafe situations, allow rest and consider debriefing; ethical care extends beyond obtaining a signed consent form. (medium confidence) — https://indeed.design/article/three-basic-principles-of-ethical-research-that-ux-can-take-from-academia/ · keywords: Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/
- [statement] Counterpoint on incentives: in a biomedical research ethics analysis, the authors argue against conventional conservatism toward payment and ask whether participants are paid enough. This is an attributed ethical argument, not an empirical estimate for UX or a universal payment rule. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5728432/
- [statement] Make participation accessible through usable research tools and alternative information formats, and budget for requested access support such as captioning, interpretation and attendant reimbursement. (medium confidence) — https://tetralogical.com/blog/2022/08/01/inclusive-user-research-recruiting-participants/ · keywords: Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://www.section508.gov/develop/usability-testing-with-people-with-disabilities/
- [statement] Cambridge’s toolkit advises that participants should still receive the offered incentive if they withdraw after beginning the study. (low confidence) — https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/
- [statement] Cambridge warns that removing names alone may not anonymize study data: characteristics, small recruitment pools and quotations can still identify participants. (low confidence) — https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/
- [statement] Cambridge advises consulting specific ethical guidance for children, people with dementia and research methods where ordinary informed consent may not be feasible; its introductory guidance is not a complete protocol for those situations. (low confidence) — https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/
- [statement] Cambridge’s toolkit recommends reporting participants fairly and accurately, listening to what they say without preconceived ideas. (low confidence) — https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/
